**Surah al-'Asr (The Declining Day)**
Three verses, Meccan

﷽

﴿By the declining day﴾

﷽

﴿By the declining day.﴾ Know that they have mentioned several opinions regarding the interpretation (*tafsir*, Qur'anic exegesis) of *al-'Asr*:

The first: that it is *al-Dahr* (time, the age). The one who holds this view has argued with several points:

The first of them: what is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he swore by *al-Dahr*, and that he (ﷺ) used to recite: "By the declining day and the calamities of time." However, we say: this would invalidate the prayer, so we do not hold that he recited it as Qur'an, but rather as an explanation. Perhaps God did not mention *al-Dahr* because He knew that the atheist is obsessed with mentioning it and glorifying it. And for this reason He mentioned it in: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time?﴾ [al-Insan: 1], as a refutation of the corruption of their saying that it is nature and time.

The second: that *al-Dahr* contains wonders, because in it there occurs happiness and hardship, health and sickness, wealth and poverty. Indeed, in it there is what is more wondrous than every wonder: that the intellect cannot bring itself to judge it as nonexistent, for it is divided and partitioned into years, months, days and hours, and it is subject to increase, decrease, correspondence, and being past and future. How, then, could it be nonexistent? Nor can one judge it to exist, because the present is not divisible, while the past and the future are nonexistent. So how is it possible to judge it as existent?

The third: that the remainder of a person's life has no value. If you wasted a thousand years and then repented in the last moment of your life, you would remain in Paradise forever and ever. Then you would know that the most noble of things is your life in that moment. Thus, time and the age are among the foundations of blessings, and for this reason He swore by it and drew attention to the fact that night and day are an opportunity that the responsible person wastes. To this the Exalted refers in His saying: ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day succeed each other for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful﴾ [al-Furqan: 62].

The fourth: that His saying in Surah al-An'am: ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To God﴾ [al-An'am: 12] refers to place and things in place. Then He said: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever dwells in the night and the day﴾ [al-An'am: 13], which refers to time and things in time. We have already explained there that time is higher and more noble than place. Since this is so, swearing by *al-'Asr* is swearing by the most noble of the two halves of God's dominion and sovereignty.

[p. 81]
The fifth: that they used to attribute loss to the calamities of time. So it is as if He swore that time and the declining day are a blessing present without any defect in them, and that the one who is lost and blameworthy is only man.

The sixth: that He mentioned the declining day, by whose passing your life is diminished. If there is no gain in exchange for it, then that diminution becomes exactly loss. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, man is in loss﴾. From this is the saying of the poet:

*We rejoice in the days as we pass them,*
*yet every day that passes is a reduction of our term.*

So the meaning is: by the declining day, whose matter is astonishing, in that a person rejoices at its passing, thinking that he has found gain, while in fact it is a destruction of his life, and indeed he is in loss.

The second opinion, which is the view of Abu Muslim: the intended meaning of *al-'Asr* is one of the two ends of the day. The reasons for this are several:

The first of them: that God swore by *al-'Asr* just as He swore by *al-Duha* (the forenoon), because both contain signs of divine power. Every morning is like the Resurrection, when people come out of their graves, the dead become living, and the scales are set up. And every evening resembles the destruction of the world by the swoon and death. Each of these two states is a witness of justice. Then, if the judge does not render judgment after the two witnesses, he is counted as one who has lost. Likewise, the human being who is heedless of these two is in loss.

The second: al-Hasan (may God have mercy on him) said: God swore by this time only to draw attention to the fact that the markets are approaching the time of their closing and the end of trade and earning in them. If you have not earned, and you have gone home and your dependents surround you, each one asking you for what is his due, then you will be ashamed and you will be among the losers. So we say: *by al-'Asr*, that is, the age of this world, the Resurrection has drawn near, and you have not yet prepared yourself, and you know that tomorrow you will be questioned about the blessings you enjoyed in your life, and you will be questioned about your dealings with creation, and every one of the wronged will claim what is yours. Then you are a loser. A parallel to this is: ﴿The reckoning of people has drawn near for them, while they are heedless and turning away﴾ [al-Anbiya': 1].

The third: that this time is honoured, and the evidence for this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever swears falsely after the 'Asr prayer, God will not speak to him and will not look at him on the Day of Resurrection." Just as He swore for the sake of the one who prospers by the forenoon, so He swore for the sake of the one who loses by the declining day. That is because He swore by the forenoon concerning the one who prospers, and the Messenger gave glad tidings that his affair is toward advancement. Here, concerning the one who loses, He threatened him that his affair is toward retreat. Then it is as if He says: some of the day remains, so He urges him to make up for what is left by repentance. It is related from one of the early Muslims: "I learned the meaning of the sura from an ice seller who used to cry out: 'Have mercy on one whose capital is melting, have mercy on one whose capital is melting.' So I said: This is the meaning of: ﴿Indeed, man is in loss﴾. The 'Asr passes over him, his life passes, and he does not earn, so he is indeed a loser."

The third opinion: the view of Muqatil, that it means the 'Asr prayer. They have mentioned several points regarding this:

The first: that the Exalted swore by the 'Asr prayer because of its excellence, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238], which in the *mushaf* (codex) of Hafsa is the 'Asr prayer. It was also said that His saying: ﴿You shall detain them after the prayer, and they swear by God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 106] refers to the 'Asr prayer.

The second: His (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever misses the 'Asr prayer, it is as if he has been robbed of his family and his property."

The third: that the obligation to perform it is more difficult, because people are busy with their trades and livelihoods at the end of the day and occupied with their earnings.

The fourth: it is narrated that "a woman used to cry out in the streets of Medina, saying: 'Direct me to the Prophet (ﷺ).' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw her and asked her what had happened. She said: 'O Messenger of God, my husband was absent from me, so I committed fornication, and a child was born to me from fornication. So I threw the child into a jar of vinegar until it died. Then we sold that vinegar. Is there any repentance for me?' He (ﷺ) said: 'As for fornication, the penalty for you is stoning. As for killing the child, its recompense is Hell. As for selling the vinegar, you have committed a great sin. But I think you have abandoned the 'Asr prayer.'" So in this hadith there is an indication of the magnification of the affair of this prayer.

The fifth: that by the 'Asr prayer the day's acts of worship are concluded. It is like repentance, by which deeds are sealed. Just as repentance is enjoined as a final counsel, so too is the 'Asr prayer, because matters are judged by their endings. So He swore by this prayer, magnifying its importance and increasing the exhortation of the responsible person to perform it, and as an indication from Him that if you perform it in its proper manner, your loss will turn into gain, as He said: ﴿Except those who believe﴾.

The sixth: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Three whom God will not look at on the Day of Resurrection, nor speak to, nor purify, and among them is counted a man who swore falsely after the 'Asr prayer."

(If it is said): the 'Asr prayer is our act, so how is it permissible to say that God swore by it?

The answer: it is not an oath because it is our act, but rather because it is a noble matter by which God has made us worship Him.

The fourth opinion: that it is an oath by the time of the Messenger (ﷺ), and they argued for this with the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The likeness of you and of those before you is like a man who hired a labourer and said: 'Who will work from dawn until noon for a qirat (a unit of reward)?' So the Jews worked. Then he said: 'Who will work from noon until the 'Asr for a qirat?' So the Christians worked. Then he said: 'Who will work from the 'Asr until sunset for two qirats?' So you worked. The Jews and the Christians became angry and said: 'We have done more work and received less pay!' God said: 'Have I diminished your wage at all?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'That is My bounty, which I give to whomever I will. You did less work and received more reward.'" This report indicates that *al-'Asr* is the time specific to him and his community. Therefore God has sworn by it. So His saying *by al-'Asr* means: by the 'Asr in which you are. In this verse He swore by His time, and in His saying: ﴿And you are a resident of this city﴾ [al-Balad: 2] He swore by His place, and in His saying: ﴿By your life﴾ [al-Hijr: 72] He swore by his life. So it is as if He said: by your time, your city, and your life, and all of that is like a container for him. If the state of the container must be magnified, then measure the state of what is contained by it. Then He directed the oath as if the Exalted were saying: "You, O Muhammad, were present among them and you called them, but they turned away from you and did not pay attention to you. How great, then, is their loss, and how mighty is their abandonment."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 103, verse 2:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾. In this there are several issues:

The first issue: The alif and lam in "al-insan" (mankind) may be for the genus (jins), or for a previously known specific referent (al-ma'hud al-sabiq). For this reason the exegetes gave two opinions:

The first: What is meant is the genus, as in the saying, "The dirham has become abundant in the hands of people." The exception of "those who believed" from "mankind" supports this view.

The second view: What is meant is a specific individual. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means a group of polytheists, such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-'As ibn Wa'il, and al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Abu Lahab. In a marfu' report it is said that it was Abu Jahl. It is related that these men used to say, "Indeed, Muhammad is in loss," so Allah, may He be exalted, swore that the matter is the opposite of what they imagined.

The second issue: Khusr (loss) is the same as khusran, as it is said: "kufr" is in "kufran" (ingratitude). Its meaning is deficiency and the loss of capital (ra's al-mal). Then there are two interpretations of this. That is because if we take "al-insan" as the genus, the meaning of loss is the ruin of one's self and one's life, except for the believer who acts righteously, for his life and wealth are not ruined, because through them he has gained everlasting happiness. If we take the word "al-insan" to refer to the disbeliever, the meaning is his being in misguidance and disbelief, except those among them who believed; then he is delivered from that loss to gain.

The third issue: He said ﴿in loss﴾ and did not say "in the loss," because indefiniteness sometimes conveys magnification (tahwil) and at other times belittlement (tahqir). If we take it in the first sense, the meaning is: indeed, mankind is in a great loss whose reality none knows except Allah. Its explanation is that sin grows in magnitude with the greatness of the one against whom it is committed, or because it occurred in return for great blessings. Both aspects are present in the servant's sin against his Lord, so that sin is indeed at the utmost of greatness. If we take it in the second sense, the meaning is that the loss of mankind is less than the loss of Satan, and in this there is good news that among My creation there is one more disobedient than you. The correct interpretation is the first.

The fourth issue: One might say: His saying ﴿in loss﴾ conveys singularity, although loss exists in various kinds.

The answer: The true loss is being deprived of serving one's Lord. As for the rest, namely deprivation of Paradise and falling into the Fire, they are in relation to the first like nothing. This is just as mankind's existence has benefits, and then He said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. That is, since this purpose is the most sublime of purposes, all other purposes are in relation to it like nothing.

Know that Allah, exalted is He, joined to this verse indications that show His emphasis in declaring that mankind is in loss:

One: His saying ﴿in loss﴾ conveys that he is as one submerged in loss, and that it has encompassed him from every side.

Second: The word "inna" (indeed), for it is for emphasis.

Third: The letter lam in "la-fi khusr" (indeed in loss).

Here there are two possibilities:

The first: In His saying ﴿la-fi khusr﴾, meaning "on the path of loss," as in His saying regarding consuming the wealth of orphans: ﴿They only consume fire into their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa': 10], since its end is fire.

The second possibility: That mankind is never free of loss, because loss is the squandering of capital, and his capital is his life, and he is seldom free of squandering his life. That is because every hour that passes over a person: if it is spent in disobedience, there is no doubt of loss; and if it is occupied with permissible things, loss is also present, because as it passed, no trace of it remained, although he was able to do with it a deed whose trace would remain forever. And if it is occupied with acts of obedience, there is no act of obedience except that it is possible to perform it, or something else, in a better way than that, because the degrees of humility and submission to Allah are infinite, just as the degrees of Allah's majesty and dominion are infinite. Whenever a person's knowledge of them is greater, his fear of Him, exalted is He, is greater, so his veneration at performing acts of obedience is more complete and perfect. Leaving the higher and settling for the lower is a kind of loss. Thus it is established that mankind is never at all free of some kind of loss.

Know that this verse is like an alert that the default state of mankind is to be in loss and failure. Its explanation: the happiness of mankind lies in love of the Hereafter and turning away from this world. Then the factors that call toward the Hereafter are hidden, while the factors that call toward love of this world are manifest: they are the five senses, desire, and anger. For this reason most of creation became occupied with love of this world, absorbed in seeking it, and so they were in loss and ruin. If it is said: He, exalted is He, said in Surah al-Tin: ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 4, 5], which indicates that the beginning is from perfection and the end is toward deficiency, while here it indicates that the beginning is from deficiency and the end is toward perfection. So how is the reconciliation?

We say: What is mentioned in Surah al-Tin concerns the states of the body, while here it concerns the states of the soul, so there is no contradiction between the two statements.

The Exalted said: ﴿Except those who have believed and done righteous deeds﴾.

Know that faith and righteous deeds have already had their explanation given many times. Now, here there are issues:

First issue: The one who argues that action is not included in the designation of faith argues that Allah the Exalted conjoined the doing of righteous deeds with faith. Had doing righteous deeds been included in the designation of faith, that would be repetition. It cannot be said that this kind of repetition occurs in the Qur'an, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7], and His saying: ﴿His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. For we say there: it was only good because its repetition indicates that it is the most noble of the kinds of that universal, and doing righteous deeds is not the most noble of the matters designated by faith, so this interpretation is void. Al-Halimi said: this repetition certainly occurs, because faith, although it does not comprise doing righteous deeds, yet His saying ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾ comprises faith, so His saying ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾ would be sufficient without mentioning His saying "those who believed." Also, His saying ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾ comprises His saying ﴿and enjoined one another to truth and enjoined one another to patience﴾, so it must be that this is repetition. The earlier scholars answered and said: We do not deny the occurrence of repetition for the sake of emphasis, but the original state is its absence, and this much suffices for the argument.

Second issue: Those who hold the threat against sinners argue from this verse. They say: the verse indicates that man is in loss absolutely, then it made an exception: ﴿except those who have believed and done righteous deeds﴾, and what is conditioned upon two conditions is absent when one of them is absent. So we know that whoever has not attained faith and righteous deeds must be in loss in this world and in the Hereafter. Since those who combine these two qualities are extremely few, and loss is necessary for whoever does not combine them, the saved are fewer than the lost. Then, even if the saved were more numerous, the fear would be great, so that you would not be among the few; how then when the saved are fewer? Should not the fear be even greater?

Third issue: This exception contains three matters:

The first: It is a consolation to the believer for the loss of his life and youth, because the deed has brought him to a good better than his life and youth.

The second: It is an alert that everything that calls you to obedience to Allah is righteousness, and everything that occupies you away from Allah with other than Him is corruption.

The third: The Mu'tazilah said: naming deeds "righteous" is an indication that the reason for their goodness is not the command, as the Ash'ariyyah say, but rather the command came because they in themselves comprise aspects of righteousness. The Ash'ariyyah answered that Allah the Exalted described them as being righteous, and did not explain that they are righteous because of aspects that return to them or because of the command.

Fourth issue: A questioner may ask: In the side of loss He mentioned the judgment and did not mention the cause, while on the side of gain He mentioned the cause, which is faith and righteous deed, and did not mention the judgment. What is the difference? We say: He did not mention the cause of loss because loss occurs by action, which is undertaking disobedience, and it also occurs by omission, which is not undertaking obedience. But gain occurs only by action, so for this reason He mentioned the cause of gain, which is deed. There is another aspect: that He, the Exalted, on the side of loss, left it general and did not detail it, while on the side of gain He detailed and clarified. This is what is fitting for generosity.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and enjoined one another to truth and enjoined one another to patience﴾.

Know that when the Exalted explained regarding those excepted that by their faith and righteous deeds they went out from being in loss and became people of happiness, inasmuch as they held fast to what leads them to success with reward and deliverance from punishment, He described them afterward as having become, due to the intensity of their love for obedience, not limiting themselves to what concerns them only, but enjoining others with the like of their way, so that they too may be a cause for the obedience of others, as the people of religion ought to be. In this sense the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a fire﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. So enjoining one another to truth includes the whole of religion, both knowledge and action, and enjoining one another to patience includes compelling the self to the hardship of the obligation in carrying out what is required and in abstaining from what is forbidden, since undertaking what is disliked and refraining from what is desired are both severely burdensome. Here there are issues:

First issue: This verse contains a severe threat, because the Exalted has judged all people to be in loss except whoever brings these four things: faith, righteous deed, enjoining truth, and enjoining patience. This indicates that salvation is conditioned upon the totality of these matters, and that just as the responsible person is obliged to attain what concerns himself, so too he is obliged in regard to others to matters including calling to religion, sincere advice, enjoining good and forbidding evil, and loving for his brother what he loves for himself. Then He repeated "enjoining" so that the first includes calling to Allah, and the second includes steadfastness upon it; the first is enjoining good and the second is forbidding evil. From this is His saying: ﴿and forbid what is wrong and bear patiently﴾ [Luqman: 17]. And Umar said: May Allah have mercy on the one who presents my faults to me.

Second issue: The verse indicates that truth is heavy, and that trials accompany it, which is why enjoining one another is joined with it.

Third issue: He said "and enjoined one another" and did not say "and they enjoin one another," so as not to make it a command; rather the purpose is to praise them for what proceeded from them in the past, and that conveys their eagerness to remain steadfast upon it in the future.

Fourth issue: Abu 'Amr recited "bi-as-sabr" with a slight rounding of the ba' (ب), a sound not fully prolonged. Abu 'Ali said: this is something permissible in pause, and does not occur in connection except by treating connection as pause, and this scarcely occurs in recitation. Upon this is what is related from Sallam ibn al-Mundhir, that he recited "wal-'asir" with a kasra on the sad (ص), and perhaps he paused due to breath running short or due to some obstacle that prevented him from running the recitation through, and this is to be understood thus, not as treating connection as pause. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best, and may Allah bless our master Muhammad (ﷺ) and his family and companions and grant them peace.
